Longitudinal Summary

Throughout 2021, the company consistently discussed free cash flow conversion as a key metric, targeting a 60% to 70% conversion of adjusted EBITDA to free cash flow before growth. Early in the year, actual operating cash flows were negative, with cash used in operating activities and investing activities, indicating cash outflows. Management reaffirmed guidance mid-year, projecting adjusted EBITDA around $3 billion with strong free cash flow conversion. By Q3, guidance for 2022 free cash flow before growth was set between $2.07 billion and $2.57 billion, including securitization proceeds. However, actual cash flows for the year showed a significant decline, with consolidated cash flows used in operations of $206 million, a sharp contrast to the prior year's positive $3.337 billion, indicating a miss relative to optimistic guidance.

Forecasting Credibility: Low

The single guidance/actual pair available shows a significant miss, with management projecting strong free cash flow conversion and positive cash flows, but the actual results revealed negative operating cash flows and overall cash used in operations for the year. This discrepancy undermines the credibility of management's forecasting on free cash flow. The lack of multiple guidance/actual pairs further limits confidence in forecasting reliability.

Q1 2021 – Q3 2021

Trends

  • Negative operating cash flows early in 2021
  • Consistent guidance on 60-70% free cash flow conversion
  • Reaffirmed and narrowed guidance mid-year
  • Inclusion of securitization proceeds in free cash flow guidance
  • Actual cash flows deteriorated significantly by year-end

Recurring Themes / Risks

  • Volatility in operating cash flows
  • Impact of securitization proceeds on free cash flow
  • Capital expenditures remaining substantial
  • Uncertainty from retail bill credits and weather events

Key Concerns

  • Significant discrepancy between optimistic free cash flow guidance and actual negative cash flows raises concerns about forecasting accuracy.
  • Depreciation and amortization reconciling adjustments vary notably quarter to quarter, which may affect cash flow interpretations.
  • The inclusion of securitization proceeds in free cash flow guidance complicates comparability and may mask underlying operational cash flow weakness.

Conclusion

The company's free cash flow performance in 2021 was weaker than management's guidance suggested, with actual operating cash flows turning negative and consolidated cash flows used in operations by year-end. Despite management's repeated emphasis on a 60% to 70% conversion of adjusted EBITDA to free cash flow before growth, the realized cash flows did not meet these expectations. The reliance on securitization proceeds to bolster free cash flow guidance further complicates the assessment of core operational cash generation. Overall, the evidence indicates that free cash flow generation was challenged in 2021, and management's forecasting on this metric demonstrated low credibility based on the available guidance and actual results.

Q2 2021
View TranscriptView 10-K/10-Q

What management said

  • "In fact, with our long-term view that we will be able to generate $3 billion or more of adjusted EBITDA, with 60% to 70% conversion of free cash flow on an annual basis, we could repurchase our entire market cap in roughly five years, if we were to allocate all of this capital to share buybacks."
  • "Next year, excluding the impact from Uri bill credit, we believe we have the ability to deliver adjusted EBITDA from ongoing operations in the $3.4 billion range with 60% to 70% conversion to free cash flow before growth."
  • "With the recent uplift in forward curves, especially in ERCOT, we continue to believe 2022 adjusted EBITDA from Ongoing Operations could be in the range of $3.4 billion, excluding the impact of the retail bill credits from Uri, with a 60% to 70% conversion to adjusted free cash flow before growth."
  • "And with the recent uptick in forward curves in both PJM and ERCOT, our forward outlook has only improved, with management expecting that we will be able to deliver strong adjusted EBITDA and adjusted free cash flow before growth in '22 and beyond."
  • "As a result, we are reaffirming our 2021 guidance ranges for both Ongoing Operations adjusted EBITDA and Ongoing Operations adjusted free cash flow before growth as set forth on Slide 6."
  • "And so, you see the free cash flow yields."
  • "We believe in the value of this business and our ability to generate significant free cash flow for allocation in the years ahead."
  • "Could that also imply that there is maybe an internal debate around a go-private scenario, if you continue to trade at these unsustainable high free cash flow yields."
  • "We believe that our relatively young low cost assets that we are de-risking will play a critical role in the energy transition for the next couple of decades, which when combined with our attractive retail and zero carbon businesses should deliver relatively consistent financial results while generating a substantial amount of free cash flow on an annual basis."
  • "We look forward to talking more about our strategic direction and how we plan to allocate our significant cash flow in the months ahead."
  • "I'm just wondering like as you go into the sort of the Q3 call and as you think through this, is there a possibility to not sell the company outright, but perhaps get a like-minded partner, who sees the value in the cash flow stream, sell a portion of the assets or a portion of companies."

Q3 2021
View TranscriptView 10-K/10-Q

What management said

  • "This represents a free cash flow conversion ratio of approximately 76%, which is higher than our historical conversion ratio due to the anticipated receipt of the securitization proceeds in the first half of 2022."
  • "We are also narrowing and revising our ongoing operations, adjusted free cash flow before growth guidance which is similarly reflected on slide 6."
  • "So turning to slide 7, Vistra is initiating its 2022 guidance today forecasting Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA in the range of $2.81 billion -$3.31 billion with ongoing operations, adjusted free cash flow before growth in the range of $2.07 to $2.57 billion."
  • "On slide 7, we also offer an illustrative view of Vistra's 2022 guidance ranges, which exclude winter storm Yuri related bill credits of approximately $185 million and also the negative in year impact from the execution of NPV positive long-dated contracts with retail customers of approximately $55 million and the $500 million of securitization proceeds in free cash flow before growth only."
  • "We are excited about this long-term capital allocation plan and believe strongly that it is the best way to maximize the value of our business as we expect we will return the majority of our free cash flow from our base business to our financial stakeholders, while being mindful of our overall leverage levels and cost effectively accelerating our renewables and battery storage growth pipeline, which should ultimately be valued at a higher multiple over time."
  • "So our illustrative guidance removes these for a more normalized view of adjusted EBITDA and adjusted free cash flow before growth, a strong conversion percentage as shown on the slide enables the significant return of capital that Curt discussed, while also supporting a strong balance sheet and the transformation of our fleet with our Vistra's zero pipelines."
  • "For our previous comments, we expect to combine project financing with renewable-related preferred equity and cash flows from existing renewable projects to cost effectively develop our current nearly five gigawatt renewable and battery pipeline over the next 5 years."
  • "Any guidance here on what you see heard as something of a more sustainable free cash flow yield?"
  • "Similarly, our guidance for Ongoing Operations Adjusted Free Cash flow before growth includes the anticipated receipt of securitization proceeds in addition to the other Yuri impacts such as bill credits."
  • "So that's not meant to be a free cash flow number if that's, I think was getting into the nature of your question, it is an EBITDA number."
  • "We believe that we have a company that's here for a long period of time, we should see that that risk premium come down and commensurately we ought to see a much lower free cash flow yield, which in turn as you know, means a higher and stronger stock price."
  • "In closing, as I hope you can see from the long-term capital allocation plan we laid out today, we believe in the value of this business and our ability to generate significant free cash flow for allocation in the years ahead."
  • "We continue to believe that Vistra will be able to convert a majority of its adjusted EBITDA to adjusted free cash flow before growth."
  • "The cash flow associated with securitization is expected to be received in the first half of 2022."
  • "And then when we look at the cash flows off of the business and the maintenance expense and things, because it's fairly low for these types of assets, we generate enough cash along with project financing, and this project capital along with our $500 million to basically self-fund the build out of the roughly five gigs through 2026."

  • "Similarly, our guidance for Ongoing Operations Adjusted Free Cash flow before growth includes the anticipated receipt of securitization proceeds in addition to the other Yuri impacts such as bill credits."
  • "We continue to believe that Vistra will be able to convert a majority of its adjusted EBITDA to adjusted free cash flow before growth."

Longitudinal Summary

Over the reported periods in 2021, the company's available liquidity fluctuated but remained in the range of approximately $2.0 billion to $2.8 billion, composed of cash on hand and available capacity under revolving credit facilities. The company consistently stated confidence in having sufficient liquidity to fund anticipated cash requirements for at least the next 12 months, supported by capital raises such as senior unsecured notes and preferred stock issuances. Liquidity changes were driven by operational cash flows, capital expenditures, share repurchases, dividends, and letters of credit. The company also noted the ongoing uncertainty related to COVID-19 as a potential risk to liquidity. No forward guidance on liquidity figures was provided, only retrospective reporting and qualitative statements about sufficiency.

Forecasting Credibility: None

There are zero guidance versus actual pairs for liquidity metrics, as management does not provide explicit forward guidance on liquidity figures. All commentary is retrospective or qualitative regarding sufficiency of liquidity. Therefore, no credibility rating can be assigned based on guidance accuracy.

Trends

  • available liquidity fluctuating around $2 billion to $2.8 billion
  • consistent internal forecasts of sufficient liquidity for 12 months
  • capital raises supporting liquidity
  • cash used in operations and capital expenditures reducing liquidity
  • COVID-19 as a liquidity risk factor

Recurring Themes / Risks

  • capital expenditures impacting liquidity
  • share repurchases and dividends reducing cash
  • letters of credit increasing liquidity usage
  • COVID-19 economic uncertainty

Key Concerns

  • No forward-looking quantitative guidance on liquidity is provided, limiting ability to assess forecasting accuracy.
  • Liquidity figures are subject to fluctuations from operational and financing activities, requiring close monitoring.
  • COVID-19 remains a noted risk that could materially impact liquidity beyond current forecasts.

Conclusion

The company maintains liquidity in the low billions, supported by cash, revolving credit facilities, and capital market issuances. Management consistently expresses confidence in having sufficient liquidity to meet cash needs for at least the next 12 months, though this is based on internal forecasts rather than explicit forward guidance. Liquidity is impacted by significant capital expenditures, dividends, and share repurchases, as well as letters of credit. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic is acknowledged as a risk that could affect liquidity. Overall, the company appears to have adequate liquidity currently, but the absence of forward guidance and the noted risks warrant continued monitoring.

  • jump to section"Vistra Operations intends to use the liquidity provided under the Commodity-Linked Facility to make cash postings as required under various commodity contracts to which Vistra Operations and its subsidiaries are parties as power prices increase from time-to time and for other working capital and general corporate purposes."
Risk Factors
  • jump to section"Volatility in market prices for fuel and electricity results from, among other factors: • demand for energy commodities and general economic conditions, including impacts of inflation and the relative strength or weakness of U.S. dollar compared to other currencies; • volatility in commodity prices and the supply of commodities, including but not limited to natural gas, coal and fuel oil; • volatility in market heat rates; • volatility in coal and rail transportation prices; • volatility in nuclear fuel and related enrichment and conversion services; • transmission or transportation disruptions, constraints, congestion, inoperability or inefficiencies of electricity, natural gas or coal transmission or transportation, or other changes in power transmission infrastructure; • severe, sustained or unexpected weather conditions, including extreme cold, drought and limitations on access to water; • seasonality; • changes in electricity and fuel usage resulting from conservation efforts, changes in technology or other factors; • illiquidity in the wholesale electricity or other commodity markets; • importation of liquified natural gas to certain markets; • development and availability of new fuels, new technologies and new forms of competition for the production and storage of power, including competitively priced alternative energy sources or storage; • changes in market structure and liquidity; • changes in the way we operate our facilities, including curtailed operation due to market pricing, environmental regulations and legislation, safety or other factors; • changes in generation capacity or efficiency; • outages or otherwise reduced output from our generation facilities or those of our competitors; 22 Table of Contents • changes in electric capacity, including the addition of new supplies of power as a result of the development of new plants, expansion of existing plants, the continued operation of uneconomic power plants due to federal, state or local subsidies, or additional transmission capacity; • local, regional, national, or global supply chain constraints or shortages; • our creditworthiness and liquidity and the willingness of fuel suppliers and transporters to do business with us; • changes in the credit risk, payment practices, or financial condition of market participants; • changes in production and storage levels of natural gas, lignite, coal, uranium, diesel and other refined products; • pandemics and epidemics (including the impacts thereto, or recovery therefrom), natural disasters, wars, sabotage, terrorist acts, embargoes and other catastrophic events; and • changes in law, including judicial decisions, federal, state and local energy, environmental and other regulation and legislation."
  • jump to section"25 Table of Contents Our liquidity needs could be difficult to satisfy, particularly during times of uncertainty in the financial markets or during times of significant fluctuation in commodity prices, and we may be unable to access capital on favorable terms or at all in the future, which could have a material adverse effect on us."
  • jump to section"With the continued tightening of credit markets that began in 2008 and expansion of regulatory oversight through various financial reforms, there has been a decline in the number of market participants in the wholesale energy commodities markets, resulting in less liquidity."
  • jump to section"31 Table of Contents Regulatory and Legislative Risks Our businesses are subject to ongoing complex governmental regulations and legislation that have adversely impacted, and may in the future adversely impact, our businesses, results of operations, liquidity, financial condition and cash flows."
  • jump to section"27 Table of Contents The agreements and instruments governing our debt, including the Vistra Operations Credit Facilities and indentures, contain restrictions and limitations that could affect our ability to operate our business, or liquidity, and results of operations, and any failure to comply with these restrictions could have a material adverse effect on us."
  • jump to section"We continue to examine the impacts of the pandemic on our workforce, liquidity, reliability, cybersecurity, customers, suppliers, along with other macroeconomic conditions and cannot currently predict whether COVID-19 will have a material impact on our results of operations, financial condition, and cash flows."
